clue.text: Chekhov offering expected to take off?

definitions.meaning: a play by Anton Chekhov, first staged in 1896
a coastal bird is one you would expect to fly off

explanation.definitionFit: Chekhov wrote a play of this title, and the bird it names is a flier that lifts off from the shore.

clue.text: River setting for The Trial?

definitions.meaning: a chalk-stream river in Hampshire, England
an examiner sets an exam, which is a trial of the candidate

explanation.definitionFit: Hampshire's famous trout river shares its name with an examination, the kind of trial one sets.

clue.text: Heroic story must be in the picture

indicators.note: the answer must be found sitting inside the words that follow, a run of their letters

explanation.surface: A heroic tale has to be in the picture, as if telling someone to stay informed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'must be in' points to letters inside 'the picture': thE PICture. 'Picture' also hints at an epic film, which misleads towards a double definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A long narrative of heroic deeds, like the Iliad, is the classic sense of the word.

clue.text: Belloc's book of Algerian impressions may it last for ever!

definitions.meaning: Hilaire Belloc's 1906 travel book about North Africa
the Latin phrase is a wish for endurance, said of Venice by Paolo Sarpi

explanation.definitionFit: Belloc took the Latin blessing for perpetual survival as the title of his Algerian travel book.

clue.text: Tell-tale German tale-teller

definitions.meaning: British slang for an informer who tells on others to the police
Günter, the German novelist who wrote The Tin Drum

explanation.definitionFit: British slang calls a police informer this, and it is the surname of the Nobel-winning German novelist.

clue.text: Some capital poems from Gavin Ewart

definitions.text: Some capital poems from Gavin Ewart

parts.words: Some capital poems from Gavin Ewart
parts.note: Gavin Ewart published a 1964 collection named for the inhabitants of the British capital; 'capital' also suggests excellent

explanation.definitionFit: Ewart's 1964 poetry collection takes its title from the people of the city where he lived.

clue.text: Graduate with church composer

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a graduate's degree

explanation.surface: A university graduate who works alongside a church composer.
explanation.definitionFit: Johann Sebastian was the great German Baroque composer of church cantatas.

clue.text: Euripides heroine had romance shattered

indicators.note: something shattered is broken into pieces, so these letters are broken and rearranged

explanation.surface: A tragic heroine of Euripides whose love affair was broken off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'shattered' rearranges the letters of HAD ROMANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Hector's widow is the title figure of a tragedy by Euripides about the aftermath of Troy.

clue.text: Falstaff's prince, extremely funny betimes, twice annually

parts.note: Prince Hal, Falstaff's drinking companion in Henry IV, later Henry V

indicators.note: the word funny is taken only at its extremes, its first and last letters

parts.note: an old word for early, in good time

explanation.surface: Shakespeare's prince, very amusing in his youth, a phrase about something occurring twice a year.
explanation.walkthrough: 'extremely' takes the first and last letters of 'funny', F and Y.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done every six months happens twice in each year.

clue.text: French music critic assents in a new composition

indicators.note: a new composition is a fresh arrangement, so the letters are put together in a new order

explanation.surface: A French critic of music approves of a newly written piece.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new composition' rearranges ASSENTS IN A; the French composer also wrote music criticism, so 'critic' is fair.
explanation.definitionFit: Camille, composer of The Carnival of the Animals, also wrote criticism on music for French journals.

clue.text: Strange Lido apparition, as he seemed to von Aschenbach

definitions.text: apparition, as he seemed to von Aschenbach

indicators.note: strange means odd or altered, so the letters are put in an unfamiliar order

explanation.surface: A strange vision on the Venice Lido, as seen by Thomas Mann's ageing writer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Strange' rearranges LIDO. In Mann's Death in Venice, Aschenbach worships the boy Tadzio as a god-like figure on the Lido beach.
explanation.definitionFit: To Aschenbach the beautiful boy Tadzio became an object of worship, a godlike vision.

clue.text: Cowardly reference to satanic types?

definitions.meaning: a play by Noël Coward, 1925, so a reference from Coward
the rebel spirits cast out of heaven with Satan

explanation.definitionFit: Noël Coward wrote a comedy with this title, and Milton's rebels thrown down from heaven bear the name.

clue.text: Would the author of such a novel be a man of letters?

definitions.text: Would the author of such a novel be a man of letters?

parts.words: Would the author of such a novel be a man of letters?
parts.note: a novel told through a series of letters makes its writer literally a man of letters

explanation.definitionFit: A novel written as an exchange of correspondence, like Richardson's Clarissa, is of this kind.

clue.text: Theatrical projection going some way to meet its audience

definitions.text: Theatrical projection going some way to meet its audience

parts.words: Theatrical projection going some way to meet its audience
parts.note: the part of a stage that juts forward past the curtain line into the auditorium

explanation.definitionFit: The forestage extends in front of the proscenium arch, reaching out towards the seated audience.

clue.text: Dreamscape of Alice and Joyce Carol?

definitions.text: Dreamscape of Alice and Joyce Carol?

parts.words: Dreamscape of Alice and Joyce Carol?
parts.note: Lewis Carroll's Alice dreams of a marvellous land, and Joyce Carol Oates wrote a 1971 novel of the same name

explanation.definitionFit: Carroll's Alice visits a magical dream realm, and Joyce Carol Oates gave that name to one of her novels.

clue.text: Sort of music provided for theatregoers?

definitions.meaning: instrumental music that tells a story or depicts a scene
the booklet sold to the audience listing cast and scenes

explanation.definitionFit: Descriptive music is called this, and so is the printed booklet given to a theatre audience.

clue.text: William Rose Benet's traders from China

definitions.text: William Rose Benet's traders from China

parts.words: William Rose Benet's traders from China
parts.note: Benét's best-known poem is about traders from Cathay, the old name for China

explanation.definitionFit: Traders who buy and sell goods are this; Benét's poem is titled after those from Cathay.

clue.text: Capital in novel has a romantic ring, being not far from Shangri La

definitions.text: Capital in novel has a romantic ring, being not far from Shangri La

indicators.note: the word in tells us the capital city sits inside the next run of words

explanation.surface: A capital city that sounds romantic in a novel because it lies near the fabled Shangri-La.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' points into 'novel has a': noveL HAS A. The rest is colour: in James Hilton's Lost Horizon, Shangri-La lies in Tibet, whose capital this is.
explanation.definitionFit: The Tibetan city, seat of the Dalai Lama, is the country's capital and lies in the region where Hilton set his hidden valley.

clue.text: 'Rising nineteen, I'll very soon be out there among the —s' (Colin MacInnes)

definitions.text: 'Rising nineteen, I'll very soon be out there among the —s' (Colin MacInnes)

parts.words: 'Rising nineteen, I'll very soon be out there among the —s' (Colin MacInnes)
parts.note: the narrator of Absolute Beginners, nearly nineteen, fears joining the ranks of older people

explanation.definitionFit: An informal word for an elderly person, which the teenage narrator dreads becoming.

clue.text: His 1981 play was sure to be a hit

definitions.text: His 1981 play was sure to be a hit

parts.words: His 1981 play was sure to be a hit
parts.note: Jack, the British dramatist, wrote a 1981 stage play titled Smash!, slang for a sure hit

explanation.definitionFit: The Manchester-born playwright's 1981 play Smash! carries a title meaning a big success.

clue.text: "I had as lief you would tell me of a mess of porridge", he said

definitions.text: "I had as lief you would tell me of a mess of porridge", he said

parts.words: "I had as lief you would tell me of a mess of porridge", he said
parts.note: a line spoken by the Welsh parson in Shakespeare's The Merry Wives of Windsor

explanation.definitionFit: The Welsh clergyman and schoolmaster in The Merry Wives of Windsor speaks this line.

clue.text: "Her — is full of money" (The Great Gatsby)

definitions.text: "Her — is full of money" (The Great Gatsby)

parts.words: "Her — is full of money" (The Great Gatsby)
parts.note: Gatsby's famous line describing how Daisy Buchanan sounds when she speaks

explanation.definitionFit: Gatsby says Daisy's way of speaking rings with wealth, the sound of her speech.

clue.text: Poet inclined to pontificate?

definitions.meaning: Alexander, the Augustan author of The Rape of the Lock
the head of the Catholic Church is the pontiff, who pontificates

explanation.definitionFit: The Augustan poet shares his name with the pontiff, the one whose role is to pontificate.

clue.text: "It — this time of year", Gogarty thought

definitions.text: "It — this time of year", Gogarty thought

parts.words: "It — this time of year", Gogarty thought
parts.note: a line by Oliver St John Gogarty, Irish poet, with the missing word a negative contraction

explanation.definitionFit: The gap takes the contracted form of 'is not', completing Gogarty's line.

clue.text: Bulwer-Lytton's schoolmaster, a male animal

parts.note: a ram is a male sheep

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist's schoolmaster described as a male beast.
explanation.walkthrough: Bulwer-Lytton's novel Eugene Aram (1832) is about a schoolmaster who turns out to be a murderer.
explanation.definitionFit: Eugene, the scholarly schoolmaster-murderer, is the title character of Bulwer-Lytton's 1832 novel.

clue.text: Weak leading men opposed to Carlyle's theme?

parts.note: anti means against or opposed to
Thomas Carlyle lectured On Heroes, Hero-Worship and the Heroic in History

explanation.surface: Feeble lead actors who stand against Carlyle's great men.
explanation.definitionFit: Protagonists lacking conventional virtues and strength are the opposite of classic champions.

clue.text: Violent ones follow violent delights, Friar Laurence warned

definitions.text: Violent ones follow violent delights, Friar Laurence warned

parts.words: Violent ones follow violent delights, Friar Laurence warned
parts.note: in Romeo and Juliet the friar says 'These violent delights have violent ...', meaning conclusions

explanation.definitionFit: Friar Laurence warns that violent delights have violent conclusions, the word for finishes.

clue.text: Modestine, perhaps, with some chaps, is on time that's the estimate

annotationWithheld.why: Modestine, perhaps, with some chaps, is on time that's the estimate: ASS (Modestine) + MEN + T are clear but no reading of 'with some' / 'is on' gives the ESS letters cleanly as held
annotationWithheld.clue: Modestine, perhaps, with some chaps, is on time that's the estimate
